title: Family of man shot dead by Hamilton police hold rally in city hall forecourt
subtitle: Renewed calls for justice come after watchdog cleared officers of wrongdoing.
article: The family of a 43-year-old man shot dead by Hamilton police is renewing calls for justice - despite the recent clearance of involved officers.

About 100 people gathered downtown Thursday night to commemorate Erixon Kabera, a father of three who died last fall after being shot multiple times on the fifth floor of his west Hamilton apartment building.
It came almost two weeks after the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) cleared two officers of wrongdoing in the shooting death.

"The SIU told us what they always say: that (the shooting) was reasonable, that it was justified, that no one will be held accountable," said Parfait Karezezi, one of Kabera's siblings. "But I stand here before you today to say no more."

The rally, organized by the Rwandan Canadian Healing Centre (RCHC), began with speeches in the city hall forecourt and ended in front of the Hamilton police station on King William Street, where a crowd had walked under a chorus of chants like "Justice for Erixon" and "No Justice, No Peace."
Seven months ago, they echoed the same chants in the same places , coming together a few days after Kabera's death to demand answers, accountability and justice for a life cut short.

"We waited more than 200 days to read a report that offered no justice, no accountability and made no sense," Dr. Ameil Joseph, an associate professor at McMaster's School of Social Work, said to the crowd.
Details of the shooting were included in the SIU's lengthy report released June 6.
Hamilton police responded to Kabera's highrise at 1964 Main St. W. after a resident called to report a man banging on her door and holding what appeared to be a black handgun.
As two officers spoke to the resident who called, Kabera exited his apartment and raised what was later confirmed to be a replica gun, according to the SIU.
Chaos ensued.

The watchdog said one officer fired up to eight rounds, while the other, mistakenly thinking his colleague's gunfire came from Kabera, unloaded six to eight. Both fell during the incident, retreating as Kabera walked toward them, the SIU said. Two attempts to deploy a conducted energy weapon (Taser) failed.

One officer - the one who started the shooting - lost her gun when she fell, according to the SIU. As Kabera continued to stride forward, the other officer reloaded his gun and fired eight more shots. Kabera then collapsed on his back.
In the report, SIU director Joseph Martino said the force used by officers was "reasonable" given Kabera was brandishing what they "honestly believed" was a real gun.
"Though mistaken, their misapprehension was a reasonable one."
Upward of 24 bullets had been fired in the incident, all from police-issued pistols, according to the SIU.
One of them inadvertently grazed an officer in the back of the head.
Kabera, meanwhile, was hit eight times - including in the neck, back, hip, arm, stomach and chest. He died in hospital just after midnight Nov. 10.
"Not one, not two, but 24 bullets they fired," said sibling Karezezi, donning a custom-made sweater of his brother's face. "He was unarmed."
Karezezi said the SIU's findings have left his grieving family with more questions than answers.
Among them is why Kabera was "immediately met with gunfire" when he stepped out into the hallway and raised the replica gun.
"At which point do they notice that he's not firing anything? They think it's a real gun, but it's not firing anything," said close friend Andy Ganza.

Karezezi noted his brother was not a criminal but a leader in the Rwandan community who respected police. He said the watchdog's findings don't clear up how Kabera - known by the nickname Gentil for his kind-hearted nature - ended up in such a violent incident.
"The biggest betrayal isn't what they did, but how they have spoken about what they did," he said in his speech to the crowd.
Karezezi added the SIU didn't call the shooting reckless.

"They called it honest belief," he said, referring to the watchdog's finding that the officers "honestly believed" Kabera had a real gun. "They didn't call it a killing; they called it understandable confusion. They didn't question the (officers') actions; they called it reasonable misperception.
"What kind of justice is that?"

In a statement shared by law firm Falconers LLP, Kabera's family said they are reviewing the report and considering legal options. A GoFundMe launched by Ganza in November has raised nearly $53,000 for legal fees.
Hamilton police said after the SIU report that it remains committed to meeting with Kabera's family and the Rwandan community to "find a path forward whenever (they're) ready."
"As a service, we recognize the profound impact this incident has had on Erixon's family, the broader community and our members."
